--- title: "October 30 – November 1, 2026" date: 2026-10-30 description: "Network median 2.91 in (range 1.81–7.64 in); peak IVT 618 kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹ from the SSW; Vance within 1,500 km" categories: [IVT ≥ 250, Tropical cyclone nearby, Snow, Final] execute: freeze: auto --- ## Summary Most of the rain fell between Saturday night, October 31, and Sunday evening, November 1, over about 19 hours. Rain gauges across Flagstaff caught a typical 2.91 inches, from 1.81 in at Flagstaff Landfill to 7.64 in at Waterline Rd #1 (Lenox-Wupatki Trails). The airport measured 3.96 in, about 25 times the normal for those 3 days. Only 2 Novembers since 1898 had a wetter 3 days. Snow fell only at the highest mountain sites; in town it was rain. Nights were mild for the season, about 12 °F above normal. The storm was fed by an atmospheric river, a long, narrow stream of moist air flowing from the south-southwest, drawn north by an area of low pressure aloft centred about 640 miles to the west-northwest. 89% of the rain fell while that stream was overhead. At its peak it carried about 2.5 times the moisture flow that defines an atmospheric river. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Technical summary Across 37 gauges the event total ranged from 1.81 to 7.64 in (median 2.91 in). The central 80% of the network-mean rain fell between Oct 31 22:00 MST and Nov 1 17:00 MST (19 h). Moisture transport over Flagstaff reached atmospheric-river strength: ERA5 IVT was at or above 250 kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹ for 24 h and peaked at 618 kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹ from the SSW at Nov 1 05:00 MST. 89% of the network-mean rain fell while IVT was at or above 250. Vance came within 1,450 km of Flagstaff (Oct 29 17:00 MST, remnant disturbance). At the IVT peak, 500-hPa flow over Flagstaff was from the SW at 35 m s⁻¹, and the 500-hPa trough axis along 35.25°N was at 120.5°W, 804 km west of Flagstaff (5,593 m, against 5,724 m over Flagstaff). A closed 500-hPa low (5,517 m) was centred 1,032 km to the WNW, at 38.5°N 122.5°W. The strongest 250-hPa wind within 1,000 km was 60 m s⁻¹, 409 km to the WSW. The 250-hPa wind over Flagstaff peaked at 57 m s⁻¹ (Nov 1 11:00 MST), 6 h after the IVT peak. ::: ## Rain across the network ::: {#5a00401f .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Event rain total at each city and county gauge (circle area proportional to total, labels in inches) over shaded relief (USGS 3DEP), 200-m elevation contours, streams (USGS NHD) and highways (Census TIGER). Step with the buttons, slider or ← → keys; space plays and pauses.* ## What the forecasters said The National Weather Service office in Flagstaff discussed the moisture source in its Area Forecast Discussions as the event unfolded. Excerpts, quoted verbatim (links to the Iowa Environmental Mesonet archive): - **Oct 29, 9:36 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202610291636)): "A deepening long-wave trough over much of the eastern Pacific will begin to draw sub-tropical moisture and remnant Monsoonal moisture northward by tonight. … By late Saturday evening, a significant tropical moisture plume originating around 24N will take aim at Arizona, as the now fully developed west coast trough starts to move inland." - **Oct 29, 10:19 PM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202610300519)): "A shortwave over the Pacific will move northeastward across Arizona, drawing northward some deep moisture with precipitable water values close to the 99th percentile for late October." - **Oct 30, 10:07 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202610301707)): "Moisture transport is underway, featuring a 20-30kt low-level jet pointed straight up the Gulf of California and into the Lower Colorado River Valley. This advection is due to a deepening trough along most of the west coast, as well as sub-tropical jet and s/wv now located around 29N/120W. … This air mass will be near records as far as PW is concerned for this time of year and the phasing of the two systems will allow for an extended period of moderate to heavy rainfall." - **Nov 1, 4:29 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202611011129)): "A concerning hydrological threat will evolve across Northern Arizona over the next 24 hours with the arrival of an atmospheric river. … Hydrological issues will be enhanced due to the already very saturated soil conditions, and it will take less rainfall than usual to cause problems." - **Nov 2, 10:08 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202611021708)): "Rain gauge and radar data suggest a widespread area 2 to 5 inches of rain (locally higher) has fallen since yesterday across and south of the Mogollon Rim, with some stream gauges exceeding record stage heights. … A record flood stage has been observed early this morning on the Little Colorado at Winslow, with the levee expected to be overtopped within the next several hours." ## Climate context - **Airport precipitation:** 3.96 in over 3 local days, against a 1991–2020 normal of 0.16 in for those days (25× normal). - **Rank:** the 3rd largest 3-day airport total in November among 129 years with data since 1898 (each year's largest 3-day total ending in November). - **Airport temperature:** highs averaged -7.3 °F and lows +12.3 °F relative to normal. - **Water year to date** (Oct 1, 2026 – Nov 1, 2026): airport 9.65 in (normal 1.57 in);
